title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hookLine: two gods race to find the end of a pillar of fire; why the lingam is a sign, and why Shivaratri is kept awake
carry: the lingam: a sign of what has no end
tomorrow: Rantideva's last cup: whose is wealth?

cards: Two gods are arguing about which of them is greater: Brahma, the creator, and Vishnu, the preserver. It's getting heated. Then, between them, a column of fire appears, with no visible top and no visible bottom.
It just goes up and down, beyond seeing. The argument stops. This is one of the best-known stories told about why the lingam is worshiped, and why some people keep Shivaratri awake all night.

teach.b: The story is told in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, and it's called the Lingodbhava, the appearance of the lingam. The two gods agree: whoever finds an end of the pillar is the greater.
Vishnu becomes a boar and digs downward. Brahma becomes a swan and flies upward.
They go for ages, and neither finds an end. Vishnu comes back and says honestly: I couldn't find it. Brahma, in many tellings, claims he did, and is caught in the lie.
Then Shiva appears from inside the pillar of fire, and in the Shaiva telling, both gods bow to something with no edges at all. That's the teaching in the lingam. Linga means a sign, a mark.

teach.h: LINGA: A SIGN, NOT A FACE.
teach.b: For Shaivas, Shiva is the one beyond every measure, and the lingam is a sign of that, not a statue of a face, because any face would be too small. Many Shaivas say Maha Shivaratri is the night that pillar appeared.
So the night is divided into four watches, called praharas, roughly three hours each.
In many temples and homes there's an abhisheka in each watch, the lingam bathed again, often with a different offering each time: milk, curd, ghee, honey, and always water.
In between, the five syllables: na, mah, shi, va, ya.

teach.h: A SIGN OF WHAT HAS NO END.
teach.b: Om Namah Shivaya. Staying awake is part of the offering: for one night, the endless matters more than sleep. And with that, the festival days are done.
Tomorrow, a king who gives away his last cup of water.

how: On Maha Shivaratri many Shiva temples and households divide the night into four watches and bathe the lingam in each, with water, milk, curd, ghee or honey, chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn; Lingodbhava images often appear on the western wall of South Indian Shiva temples.

o: a night of lamps for the goddess of wealth
the great night of Shiva, kept in four watches
the morning a god's statue is carried to the sea

games.q: the pillar of fire — tap the pairs.
p: becomes a boar and digs down
becomes a swan and flies up
one of the night's four watches

s: Vishnu finds the bottom of the pillar
he digs for ages, finds no end, and says so honestly.
many Shaivas say Shivaratri is the night the pillar of fire appeared
it's one of the main reasons given for the vigil.
the night is often divided into four watches with an abhisheka in each
the praharas, each with its own bathing of the lingam.

games.q: you're Vishnu. you've dug for ages and found no bottom to the pillar of fire. Brahma is back from above. what do you say?
games.why: Vishnu admits he found no end. in many tellings Brahma claims he did, and is caught in the lie.

practice: If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya silently, once with each breath, the way the vigil does through the night. If not, follow one breath all the way in, looking for where it begins, and all the way out, looking for where it ends.
Neither god found the pillar's end, and you may not find an edge either. When you want to stop, stay three breaths longer.

wordCard.voice: Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, kept in four watches, and remembered by many as the night the pillar of fire appeared, with no end either way.

orig.note: Sanskrit liṅga (sign, mark) + udbhava (appearance, arising): the lingam's appearance as a pillar of fire.

carryVoice: Your line: the lingam, a sign of what has no end. Day six hundred eighty-nine, done.
